claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure composed of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Continuous internal lamellar-colony boundaries foster dislocation pile-ups.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries generate local stress concentrations.
These local stress concentrations promote microcracking and brittle or catastrophic failure during straining.
A short-duration, high-temperature rapid thermal anneal can induce localized recrystallization at internal boundaries.
Rapid thermal annealing will modify the continuous internal boundaries of the lamellar colonies.
The treatment will produce recrystallized or locally modified boundaries that accumulate lower dislocation densities.
The thermal pulse will form more equiaxed micro-regions along the lamellar boundaries.
Boundary recrystallization or relaxation will reduce barriers to dislocation motion and limit dislocation pile-ups.
Limiting dislocation pile-ups will decrease local stress concentrations and delay premature microcracking.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy, including delayed necking and greater elongation to failure.
The treated alloy will maintain or potentially increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Preservation of fine structural features will enable strength retention or improvement after annealing.
The proposed benefits apply during room-temperature tensile testing at quasi-static strain rates.
The beneficial effects will be highly sensitive to annealing time and temperature.
Over-annealing can cause excessive recrystallization and grain growth that reduce strength.
The processing window that modifies boundaries without compromising strength is narrow.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome treats unchanged yield strength as successful strength retention, whereas the falsification rule includes unchanged yield strength among the conditions for rejection.
